label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
claim: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
quote: all processes, whether they are produced by human effort or occur spontaneously in nature, can be viewed as computations.
scope: all natural and artificial processes
candidate_data: none known

label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
claim: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
quote: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.
scope: essentially all processes in nature, mathematics and engineered systems whose behavior is not obviously simple
measurable_quantities: fraction of non-simple rules in an enumerated class proven universal
computational equivalence (mutual emulability) of processes
candidate_data: Exhaustive enumerations of elementary and totalistic cellular automata and small Turing machines run with Wolfram Language or other open simulators, together with the published literature on universality proofs.

label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
claim: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
quote: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.
scope: enumerable classes of simple programs such as cellular automata, Turing machines and related systems
measurable_quantities: number of rules in a class with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior
number of those rules proven universal or proven non-universal
candidate_data: Enumerations of elementary and small totalistic cellular automata and small Turing machines, compared against published universality proofs such as that for rule 110.

label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
claim: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
quote: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.
scope: all physical systems in our universe, including computers and brains
measurable_quantities: existence of any physical device that decides a Turing-undecidable problem
candidate_data: none known

label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
claim: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
quote: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.
scope: rules governing natural systems not constrained by engineering or natural selection
measurable_quantities: statistical properties of rules inferred for natural systems compared with random rule ensembles
candidate_data: none known

label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
claim: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
quote: So far as I can tell, all possible blocks eventually appear, potentially letting the pattern serve as a kind of directory of all possible computations.
scope: rule 30 elementary cellular automaton started from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: for each block length k, the number of distinct length-k blocks occurring in the first t steps
step at which each block first appears
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 30 with Wolfram Language or open-source cellular automaton code; OEIS entries on the rule 30 pattern and center column.

label: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
claim: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.
quote: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.
scope: analog computers, continuous mathematical models, and physical systems treated as continuous
measurable_quantities: computational power of analog devices relative to digital computers
precision and noise limits in analog computation
candidate_data: Published literature on analog computation and real-number models of computation; no specific dataset known.

label: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claim: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.
quote: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.
scope: equations built from standard mathematical functions
candidate_data: Published results in mathematical logic on decidability of equations over the reals with trigonometric functions.

label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
claim: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
quote: while in simple cases complicated molecules may for example arrange themselves in configurations that minimize energy, the evidence is that in more complicated cases they typically do not.
scope: molecular configurations such as large biomolecules and glasses
measurable_quantities: energy of observed molecular conformations relative to computed global minima
occurrence of kinetically trapped or metastable states
candidate_data: Protein Data Bank structures compared with energy-minimization and folding-simulation results, and published studies of glassy and metastable molecular states.

label: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
claim: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.
scope: human brains and thinking
measurable_quantities: complexity of mechanistic models needed to reproduce human cognitive behavior
candidate_data: none known

label: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
claim: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.
quote: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct
scope: simple programs with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior, such as rule 30
measurable_quantities: statistical randomness test results on rule 30 output
success of compression or prediction methods on such patterns
universality status of rule 30
candidate_data: Rule 30 center-column sequences (OEIS) analyzed with standard randomness test suites such as NIST SP 800-22 or TestU01.

label: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
claim: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.
quote: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.
scope: observers (human or otherwise) studying systems in nature and simple programs
candidate_data: none known

label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
claim: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
quote: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.
scope: any system whose evolution is computationally irreducible
measurable_quantities: computational cost of the fastest known method to obtain the state after t steps, as a function of t
candidate_data: Benchmarks of algorithms for computing cellular automaton states after t steps (e.g. rule 30 center column) using open simulation tools.

label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
claim: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
quote: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.
scope: all systems, especially simple programs
measurable_quantities: existence of sub-linear-time procedures for computing states of repetitive, nested and other cellular automata
candidate_data: Enumerations of elementary cellular automata classified by behavior, with known closed-form or fast algorithms for additive and nested rules.

label: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
claim: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.
quote: this, I believe, is the fundamental reason that traditional theoretical science has never managed to get far in studying most types of systems whose behavior is not ultimately quite simple.
scope: theoretical science and mathematical modeling
candidate_data: none known

label: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
claim: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.
quote: there are many common systems whose behavior cannot in the end be determined at all except by something like an explicit simulation.
scope: common natural and artificial systems with complex behavior
candidate_data: none known

label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
claim: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.
quote: In general, to find the color of a cell after t steps of rule 188 or rule 60 evolution takes about Log[2, t] steps.
scope: elementary cellular automata rules 60 and 188, and nested patterns generally
measurable_quantities: steps needed to compute cell color at step t
agreement with direct simulation
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rules 60 and 188 alongside digit-based fast procedures (e.g. Lucas's theorem for rule 60) using open tools.

label: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
claim: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.
quote: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.
scope: systems with complex-looking behavior in nature and among simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of complex-looking rules in an enumerated class for which a fast (polylog or sub-linear) evaluation procedure exists
candidate_data: Enumerations of small cellular automata searched for fast evaluation procedures using open simulation tools.

label: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
claim: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
quote: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.
scope: human brains and other systems that appear to exhibit free will
measurable_quantities: predictability of decisions from neural measurements
candidate_data: none known

label: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
claim: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.
quote: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.
scope: systems with complex behavior, including simple programs and natural systems
candidate_data: Published undecidability results for cellular automata and tiling problems.

label: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
claim: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.
quote: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.
scope: 4-color totalistic cellular automaton with code 1004600 and simple programs generally
measurable_quantities: steps until each pattern dies out
pattern width after 10^6 and 10^7 steps
candidate_data: Direct simulation of totalistic code 1004600 with Wolfram Language or open cellular automaton software.

label: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
claim: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.
quote: I strongly suspect that even with just three pairs there is already computational irreducibility
scope: Post Correspondence Problem instances with small numbers of pairs
measurable_quantities: length of minimal solutions for small instances
decidability status for 3-pair instances
candidate_data: Published decidability results for bounded-size Post Correspondence Problem instances and computer searches of small instances.

label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
claim: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.
quote: it turns out that the only rates of growth that one ever sees are linear, square and exponential.
scope: all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors, under Wolfram's halting convention
measurable_quantities: maximum steps to halt as a function of input length for each machine
set of functions computed (351)
candidate_data: Exhaustive simulation of 2-state 2-color Turing machines using Wolfram Language TuringMachine or open-source enumerators.

label: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort
claim: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.
quote: there are indeed Turing machine computations that cannot actually be carried out except by spending an amount of computational effort that can increase exponentially with the length of input.
scope: Turing machines with up to 4 states and 2 colors
measurable_quantities: minimum over all machines of size at most 4 states of maximum steps for a given function, versus input length
candidate_data: Exhaustive enumeration of 3- and 4-state 2-color Turing machines with open or Wolfram Language simulators.

label: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
claim: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.
quote: almost all the very varied systems in this book can actually be made to emulate each other in a quite comparable number of steps.
scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, register machines, substitution systems and other simple programs
measurable_quantities: slowdown factor of explicit emulations between system types
candidate_data: Explicit emulation constructions in the theory-of-computation literature and direct simulation of them.

label: P is likely different from NP
claim: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.
quote: And although it has never been established for certain it seems by now likely that in most meaningful senses there is not.
scope: computational complexity of problems about multiway systems and non-deterministic Turing machines
candidate_data: none known

label: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
claim: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.
quote: my expectation is that asking about possible outcomes of t steps of evolution will already be NP-complete even for the rule 30 cellular automaton
scope: rule 30 cellular automaton and simple instances of NP-complete problems
measurable_quantities: runtime scaling of best SAT solvers on rule 30 preimage problems as t increases
candidate_data: Rule 30 preimage instances encoded as SAT and run with open SAT solvers such as those from the SAT Competition.

label: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact
claim: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.
quote: I strongly suspect that even if this is formally the case, it will still not turn out to be a true representation of ultimate physical reality
scope: quantum computation and the fundamental physics of our universe
measurable_quantities: demonstrated scaling of quantum algorithms versus best classical algorithms on large instances
candidate_data: Published quantum-advantage experiments and their classical-simulation rebuttals.

label: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution
claim: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.
quote: there really can in some fundamental sense be an almost exponential difference in the amount of computational effort needed to find the behavior of a system with given particular initial conditions, and to solve the inverse problem of determining which if any initial conditions yield particular behavior.
scope: systems with complex behavior, including cellular automata
measurable_quantities: forward simulation cost versus best preimage-search cost as a function of t
candidate_data: Benchmarks of cellular automaton forward simulation versus SAT-solver-based preimage computation using open tools.
